title: How We Scaled Ligerio to €10M Revenue — Operations, Logistics and Systems in a 2.5-Tonne Average Order Business
excerpt: Ligerio sells heavy flooring and wall coverings online — average order weight: 2.5 tonnes. We scaled from near-zero to €10M revenue in 4 years with 50–100% YoY growth. Here is what we built operationally to make that possible.
content:
# How We Scaled Ligerio to €10M Revenue — Operations, Logistics and Systems in a 2.5-Tonne Average Order Business

Selling flooring and wall coverings online sounds straightforward until you realise the average order weighs 2.5 tonnes. This is not a book or a T-shirt. It is a pallet — sometimes several — that has to move from a supplier warehouse in France or Italy to a building site, an apartment renovation, or a professional workshop. Coordinating that at scale, with quality and without proportionally expanding your team, is the core operational challenge at Ligerio.

I joined Ligerio as co-founder in 2021, when Jean de Varine — whom I had met years earlier at Rocket Internet in West Africa — was already building the foundation. Over the following four years, we scaled from near-zero to €10M+ in annual revenue, achieving 50–100% year-on-year growth for three consecutive years. We reached break-even in March 2024. We built a team of 40+. And we exited in mid-2025.

This is not a fundraising story. It is an operations story.

---

## Starting with a Wix site and 10 product references

The early version of Ligerio was intentionally minimal. A simple website, a limited catalogue, dropshipping as the initial model. The logic was correct: before building infrastructure, you need to understand what customers actually buy, how they buy, and where the friction is. Dropshipping — where the supplier ships directly to the end customer — is a legitimate MVP model for a heavy-goods e-commerce business. Your working capital requirement is close to zero. You test demand without committing to stock.

But dropshipping has a ceiling. When the volume grows, supplier lead times vary, delivery tracking is opaque, and the customer experience suffers. You are entirely dependent on suppliers' logistics capacity, which was not built to handle the throughput of a growing e-commerce brand.

The market itself is vast but fragmented. The French renovation and flooring market is valued at approximately €13 billion. Buying quality flooring online remains difficult: the products are heavy, bulky, relatively expensive, and require expertise to match specifications. Ligerio's thesis was that digitising this market — with better content, cleaner UX, and reliable logistics — was a structural opportunity.

---

## The logistics constraint is the business constraint

In most e-commerce, logistics is a cost line. In flooring, logistics is the product. A customer ordering 40m² of stone flooring is not just buying tiles — they are buying the certainty that the right product will arrive intact, on time, at the right address, with the right documentation. One broken pallet, one wrong reference, one missed delivery window can derail a renovation project entirely.

This creates a very specific operational challenge: **the quality bar for logistics execution is higher than in most e-commerce verticals**, while the complexity per order is dramatically higher. Suppliers are often small manufacturers who lack sophisticated logistics setups. Carriers who handle pallets and heavy freight are not the same as parcel couriers. And the customer — whether a private individual or a professional artisan — has no margin for error.

We had to build systems that could manage this complexity across a growing volume of orders, across a growing number of suppliers, without proportionally growing the operational headcount.

---

## The model shift: from dropshipping to consignment

The pivot that changed our operating model was the move from dropshipping to consignment on our best-sellers — and, progressively, to stocking in our own warehouse.

Consignment is a hybrid model: the supplier delivers a stock of goods to Ligerio, which remains the supplier's property until sold. We bear the logistics and the customer relationship; the supplier retains ownership until sale. For a capital-light business, this is significantly better than dropshipping (we control delivery quality) without requiring the full working capital of traditional stocking.

We were deliberate about where to apply each model. Consignment makes sense on products where you already have reliable demand data — your proven best-sellers, your highest-velocity references. You do not immobilise stock for months on uncertain products. You run consignment on what you know sells, and you test new references in dropshipping until the data justifies the commitment.

This discipline — applying the right supply model to each product category based on velocity data — was one of the key operational levers behind our growth without proportional cost inflation.

---

## Scaling logistics throughput without scaling the team

The metric I am most proud of at Ligerio is not the revenue. It is the logistics throughput improvement.

Over three years, we multiplied our logistics capacity by 20x — the volume of orders processed, coordinated and delivered — without a proportional increase in our operational headcount. The business scaled; the team did not scale at the same rate.

How? Several levers worked in combination:

**Supplier integration.** We built structured processes for supplier communication: standardised order formats, automated status updates, clear escalation paths for exceptions. The less manual the supplier interface, the more volume our small ops team could manage.

**Carrier specialisation.** Heavy-freight logistics is a niche. We worked to identify and build relationships with carriers who actually understood pallet delivery to private individuals — which is much harder than B2B freight. This reduced damage rates and delivery failures.

**Process documentation and repeatability.** Every exception that happened once was documented and turned into a playbook. The goal was to remove the dependence on institutional memory: any team member should be able to handle a supplier issue, a damaged delivery claim, or a return, by following a clear process.

**Tooling.** We invested in the right tools to create visibility across orders, stock, suppliers and carriers. Not custom-built software — pragmatic tool choices that gave us real-time status across the order lifecycle without requiring manual data entry.

The result: a small, effective ops team that could handle a volume that would normally require a much larger headcount.

---

## SEO as a growth engine

Our acquisition strategy was heavily SEO-focused — not because we ignored paid channels, but because the economics of SEO compound in a way that paid acquisition does not.

We built what we internally called a "war room" approach to SEO: systematic, data-driven, combining human editorial judgment with AI-assisted production. The goal was to create genuinely useful content for people planning a renovation — not keyword stuffing, but real advice on how to choose flooring, how to match materials, how to estimate quantities.

The results were significant: we grew to 200,000+ monthly website visitors and managed an annual acquisition budget of approximately €400k. Reaching 100,000 organic clicks was a milestone that required real organisational investment — SEO at this level is not a side project, it is a full operational function.

For a business where average order values are high and purchase cycles are long (someone planning a full renovation takes time before buying), SEO delivers the right kind of traffic: people in research mode, building consideration, who will convert when they are ready.

---

## Building a B2B channel without breaking the B2C model

At launch, Ligerio was designed for private individuals. But professionals — architects, interior designers, renovation contractors — naturally found us. They were buying the same products, but in larger quantities, with different requirements: trade pricing, faster delivery, credit terms, dedicated support.

By the time of our seed round in late 2022, approximately 40% of our customers were professionals. This was not a planned pivot — it was a signal from the market that we listened to and built around.

The challenge is that B2B and B2C are operationally different: different purchase journeys, different customer needs, different service levels. We had to design a model that served both without compromising either. The answer was progressive specialisation — dedicated flows, dedicated pricing, dedicated account management — while keeping the core infrastructure (catalogue, logistics, CRM) shared.

---

## The seed round: €3.9M from Go Capital and BPI

In November 2022, we closed a €3.9M seed round with Go Capital (Loire Valley Invest fund), BPI France, and a strong group of business angels — including Sébastien de Lafond (MeilleursAgents), the Deconinck family (major shareholders in Tarkett), Clément Ouizille (Convelio), and Folco Aloisi (Karavel group).

The rationale was expansion: new product categories, deeper supplier relationships, acceleration of the B2B channel, and continuing to invest in technology. The ambition at the time was to reach €50M in annual revenue with 10,000+ references in the catalogue.

Reaching break-even in March 2024 — after this first funding round, in a difficult macro environment for e-commerce — was a proof point for the operational model. We were not burning cash indefinitely. The business had real unit economics.

---

## What Ligerio taught me about operations at scale

Four years building Ligerio in the specific context of heavy-goods e-commerce left me with a few durable convictions.

**Constraint is a forcing function for systems thinking.** The 2.5-tonne average order is not a bug — it is a feature. It forced us to build real logistics infrastructure, real supplier relationships, real quality controls. Businesses that cannot hide behind easy logistics tend to build better operations.

**You do not need to hire your way out of volume.** The 20x logistics throughput improvement without proportional headcount growth was not magic. It was the result of systematically replacing manual coordination with documented processes and appropriate tooling. Every operator I have worked with since has a version of the same problem: manual work masquerading as a legitimate cost of doing business.

**The right supply model per product category is a strategic lever.** Too many e-commerce businesses treat supply as a single model across the whole catalogue. Segmenting by velocity, margin, and strategic importance — and applying dropshipping, consignment, or stocking accordingly — is a genuine competitive advantage.

**SEO is an operations project, not a marketing project.** Getting to 200k+ monthly visitors required process, tooling, editorial discipline and sustained effort over time. Treating it as a campaign rather than an operating function is how most companies underperform on organic search.

---

## What came next

I left Ligerio in mid-2025 — on good terms, with the company in a strong position. The operational foundation was solid, the team was in place, and Jean de Varine, CEO from the beginning, continues to lead the company.

The experience at Ligerio directly informed what I am building now at [Moverz](https://moverz.fr) — an AI-driven pricing and operations engine for the moving services market. A different industry, but the same core challenge: a fragmented, high-complexity market where the winner will be the player who builds the best operational infrastructure.

If you are building or scaling a business with operational complexity — logistics, suppliers, multi-channel, heavy coordination — and you want to discuss systems, I am available at [gdetaisne@gmail.com](mailto:gdetaisne@gmail.com).

---

*This article references the [Le Panier podcast episode #286](https://lepanier.io/10m-de-ca-en-5-ans-en-vendant-des-materiaux-de-construction/) (May 2024) and the [FrenchWeb coverage](https://www.frenchweb.fr/seed-e-commerce-ligerio-leve-39-millions-deuros-aupres-de-go-capital-et-de-business-angels/437388) of Ligerio's seed round.*

title: Why C-level executives can’t perform anymore without deeply understanding technology
excerpt: For years, top executives could be excellent without really understanding technology. That world is gone. Today, products are digital, distribution is digital, data is everywhere and AI is rewriting value chains. A C-level who doesn’t understand tech in depth becomes a bottleneck – even if they are brilliant on the P&L.
content:
# Why C-level executives can’t perform anymore without deeply understanding technology

For years, senior executives could be excellent without really understanding technology. Finance owned the numbers, operations owned the teams, and “IT” owned the tools. That world is gone. Today, products are often software, distribution is digital, data is everywhere and AI is starting to rewrite value chains. In this context, a C-level who doesn’t understand tech in depth becomes a bottleneck – even if they are brilliant on the P&L.

According to McKinsey, **around 70% of digital transformations fail** to deliver the expected value, often due to a lack of real sponsorship and digital skills at the top. Research from the MIT Center for Information Systems Research shows that companies whose boards are “digitally savvy” enjoy **30–40% higher revenue growth and value creation** than their peers. In other words, technological competence at leadership and board level is no longer a bonus – it is a measurable performance driver.

---

## 1. Without tech literacy, leaders are flying blind

Not understanding tech today is not just about “not knowing how to code”. It means being blind to three fundamental dimensions of leadership: how systems really work, how reliable the data is, and where the real risks lie. When a C-level doesn’t understand how their systems work, they depend on internal “translators” for everything: why a KPI is moving, why a project takes six months instead of six weeks, why teams insist on a rebuild instead of another feature. This gap is costly: slower decisions, biased trade-offs, poorly framed projects.

A leader without tech literacy sees only the screens, not the flows behind them. They discuss KPIs without understanding how they are constructed, AI without seeing the training data, security without visualising the attack surface. As the organisation grows, the time needed to “understand what is really going on” explodes – and tech teams quietly learn to work around the top management instead of with it.

- **Without understanding systems**, a leader sees only interfaces, not dependencies (what talks to what, where data is lost, where costs explode).
- **Without understanding data**, they make decisions on top of reporting whose limits they can’t see (lag, bias, missing history, hand-rebuilt series).
- **Without understanding architectures**, they underestimate the real cost of change (necessary refactors, technical debt, security, team bandwidth).
- **Without understanding realistic AI use cases**, they either overhype or underuse it: gadgets and PoCs on one side, irrecoverable lag on the other.

This is exactly what Harvard Business Review and MIT Sloan keep pointing out: leaders who don’t understand technology depend more on internal narratives than on system reality – and their strategic decisions suffer.

---

## 2. What “deeply understanding technology” really means (and doesn’t)

We often confuse two notions: **being a CTO** and **being a tech-savvy C-level**. A CFO, COO or CEO doesn’t need to become a cloud architect, but they can no longer afford to have only a superficial view. The goal is not to write every line of code; it is to think in systems, challenge technical choices and understand orders of magnitude for cost and risk.

For a C-level, “deeply understanding technology” means very concrete things:

- **Thinking in systems**: being able to mentally map flows (customers → product → invoicing → cash), dependencies (CRM, line-of-business tools, ERP, bank, BI) and friction points. Being able to ask: *“If we change this here, what breaks over there?”*.
- **Understanding the main technical building blocks**: without going into code, knowing what monoliths, microservices, APIs, data warehouses, integrations and AI models imply. Not to build them, but to understand their cost, rigidity and speed of evolution.
- **Reading data with intelligent scepticism**: asking the right questions: where does this data come from? How often is it updated? What don’t we see? What is the realistic error range? Many governance failures stem from leaders who don’t know how to spot weak signals in their systems.
- **Understanding genuine AI productivity levers**: distinguishing between use cases where AI is structurally meaningful (back-office automation, classification, forecasting, internal copilots) and those where it is still a gadget. Knowing what this requires in terms of data, security and change management.

Schools like Harvard, Stanford or CentraleSupélec increasingly emphasise this hybrid competence in their executive programmes: not to turn CxOs into developers, but into **decision architects** able to talk eye-to-eye with tech teams.

---

## 3. Why this is critical for CFOs and COOs in particular

For a CFO or COO, technology is not just another topic. It **is** the connective tissue of finance and operations: what makes numbers land on time, teams know what to do and customers experience a consistent journey. A CFO/COO without tech literacy is, by design, behind what is really happening in the business.

When a CFO/COO doesn’t master tech, reporting is slow, fragile and patched together; teams spend their time reconciling spreadsheets instead of running the business; IT projects are seen as “costs” rather than structural changes. A tech-savvy CFO/COO, on the contrary, can play a very different role.

- **Designing a genuine operating system for the company**: a backbone tying together CRM, orders, inventory, invoicing, treasury, accounting and support. When this backbone is well designed, numbers “come up on their own”, alerts are automated and decisions rely on live data.
- **Massively automating low-value work**: bank reconciliation, invoice chasing, margin checks are perfect candidates for workflow + AI. A tech-savvy CFO/COO doesn’t just ask for “a tool”: they can specify rules, required data and exceptions.
- **Redefining internal roles**: instead of stacking layers of middle-management and back-office, they redesign roles around decisions and exceptions, while letting the system handle routines. This is exactly the promise of projects like Moverz: delivering the service level of a profitable 50-person company… with no employees, powered by systems.
- **Speaking the language of investors and family offices**: the most advanced funds know that value lies in systems. A CFO/COO able to clearly explain architecture, data, AI and automation levers reassures not only on the P&L but on operational resilience.

World Economic Forum data is clear: by 2027, **around 60% of workers will need significant reskilling**, with digital and analytical skills consistently at the top of the list. If finance and ops leadership is not ahead of this curve, it will inevitably lag behind its own organisation.

---

## 4. What research says (Harvard, MIT, McKinsey, WEF…)

Several streams of research converge on one point: **organisations with digitally savvy leaders outperform others**. This is now documented beyond anecdotes, with numbers.

- **MIT CISR – digital boards**: companies whose boards include several digitally savvy members show 30–40% higher revenue growth and value creation than their peers, with stronger margins.
- **McKinsey – digital transformation failure**: in “Unlocking success in digital transformations”, McKinsey notes that around 70% of digital transformations fail to create the expected value. Success factors include strong top-management involvement, a willingness to rethink operating models, and investment in digital skills at leadership level.
- **Harvard / Stanford – leadership and disruption**: Harvard Business Review and Stanford’s Technology Ventures Program underline that leaders who understand disruptive technologies (cloud, data, AI) are the ones who manage to transform their organisations without breaking them: they know where to experiment, where to industrialise, and where not to touch.
- **World Economic Forum – skills of the future**: the WEF shows that analytical thinking, digital literacy and understanding of AI are among the most requested skills for leaders – not as cosmetic “nice-to-haves”, but as core abilities to redesign work and value chains.

All these sources point in the same direction: technology is no longer a support function; it is a language. Leaders who don’t speak that language increasingly depend on those who do – internally or at competitors.

---

## 5. How a C-level can realistically become tech-savvy

The good news is that this competence **can be learned**, even for profiles strongly oriented towards finance, operations or strategy. It is less a matter of age than of exposure, discipline and intellectual humility. More and more executives are going “back to school”, through executive programmes or deeper degrees.

A few concrete levers for a C-level:

- **Take a structured programme, not just attend conferences**: executive education at Harvard, Stanford, MIT, CentraleSupélec… or, as I do, a Computer Science degree at Harvard. The idea is not to collect certificates, but to confront the rigour of the discipline (algorithms, data, systems).
- **Work on real products and tools, not just mock-ups**: co-designing or even coding internal tools (even simple ones) changes how you think. You see what is trivial, what is complex, what is expensive, what is fragile. A C-level who has deployed an internal tool or automation end-to-end never looks at IT projects the same way.
- **Spend time inside systems with tech/data teams**: instead of consuming only PowerPoint summaries, sit with developers and data engineers, look at raw dashboards, logs and architecture diagrams. Ask naïve questions, and accept not understanding everything at first.
- **Index leadership practice on technology**: for each strategic decision (new country, new product, M&A, cost cutting), systematically ask: which systems does this impact? What data is needed to steer this decision? Which part of this decision can be augmented by AI or automation?

The logic is simple: the more a C-level is exposed to system reality, the less dependent they are on technical storytelling – and the faster and sharper their decisions become.

---

## 6. Towards “full-stack” C-levels: finance, ops, tech, AI

We often talk about “full-stack” developers. But the real challenge for the coming years is **“full-stack” C-levels**: executives able, in the same meeting, to move from a gross-margin issue to a data-schema question, from an architecture dilemma to a cost-reduction plan, from a product detail to a board discussion.

A CFO/COO who:

- has operated in extreme contexts (Jumia, Glossybox, Ligerio…);
- can build or specify systems themselves (TypeScript, AI, automation);
- and deepens this competence through a Computer Science curriculum at Harvard;

sends a very clear signal to the market: **“I don’t lead by gut feeling, I lead through systems.”**

For funded scale-ups and family offices, this is exactly the profile that makes the difference: someone who can take over in a crisis *and* **design the machine** that will prevent the same crisis from happening again – finance, operations, tech and AI in the same head.

---

## Further reading

- **Harvard Law School – Corporate Governance Forum**: *How board and C-suite collaboration can build organizational resilience*  
  https://corpgov.law.harvard.edu/2025/10/22/how-board-and-c-suite-collaboration-can-build-organizational-resilience/
- **Stanford Technology Ventures Program** – Leadership and disruptive technologies  
  https://stvp.stanford.edu/videos/leadership-and-disruptive-technologies-entire-talk/transcript-pdf-leadership-and-disruptive-technologies-entire-talk
- **World Economic Forum – Future of Jobs Report** (latest edition)  
  https://www.weforum.org/reports/the-future-of-jobs-report-2023/
- **CentraleSupélec – Computer science programmes for engineers and leaders**  
  https://www.centralesupelec.fr/programmes/ingenieur-specialite-informatique
